resources.string: Human thyroid feedback on the pituitary
How a neuron passes on a signal
An example of chemical synaptic transmission. Signals, colors, and timing are illustrative, not neurological test results.
A neuron integrates inputs on its dendrites and cell body. When the axon initial segment reaches threshold, it can fire an action potential.
The signal travels down the axon
An action potential travels down the axon to its terminal. It is a change in membrane voltage, not neurotransmitter flowing down the axon.
Calcium channels open at the terminal
Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels at the terminal, allowing calcium to enter from outside.
Calcium promotes fusion of transmitter-filled vesicles with the presynaptic membrane. Released transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors.
Activated receptors can change electrical activity in the next cell. This example shows excitation; the transmitter is then cleared by uptake, breakdown, or diffusion.
How myelin helps nerve signals travel
A qualitative example with equal-length axons, not to scale or an estimate of conduction speed. Not all axons are myelinated.
In the brain and spinal cord, one oligodendrocyte can extend processes that form myelin on segments of different axons.
In peripheral nerves, a myelinating Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon in multiple insulating layers.
Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between neighboring myelin segments. Exposed axon membrane at the nodes is rich in channels that regenerate an action potential.
The signal is regenerated at each node
Local current travels within the axon beneath myelin. The action potential is regenerated at the next node; it does not jump through extracellular space.
In this equal-length illustration, the signal travels farther in the myelinated axon. Actual speed also depends on factors such as axon diameter.
How the thyroid feedback loop works
A representative feedback loop, not an estimate of personal thyroid results or advice about medication.
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) travels from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary through portal vessels.
In response to TRH, the anterior pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). In the blood, TSH acts on the thyroid gland.
The thyroid releases T4 and T3
TSH stimulates follicular cells to make and release thyroid hormones. The gland releases mostly T4 and some T3.
Some T4 is converted in tissues
Thyroid hormones travel in the bloodstream. Some T4 is converted into the more active T3 in other tissues.
When thyroid hormone rises, negative feedback reduces TRH and TSH release from the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.
